This has been answered already in this thread, but to give a more detailed breakdown of what happened:

Baby Boomers want a house:

So, they get a loan. There is associated risk in giving the loan, and the banks weigh this risk before offering it. People who are capable of paying their loan are considered low risk and are charged low interest rates. People who may not be able to pay are high risk and are charged high interest rates.

Banks want to make more money

So they increase the risk of their portfolio. This means offering more loans to risky people. Now the issue is that when these people stop paying their loans, the banks now are not making money, and instead have to pay taxes, maintenance, and general upkeep of the property. And, being a bank in 2008, they don't actually have 100% of the funds in a vault. So if enough of these risky people default, the bank actually won't have enough to pay back the money that they owe other people. This is a risk in banks, and is why we have government regulations on them. It is also why we have the FDIC, so unscrupulous people don't just gamble away everyone's savings

Banks don't want to hold all this risk

Now, because the banks have obligations to pay themselves, holding a lot of risk is not good. So they sell the mortgages to other investors, so if the people default, the investors and not the banks, would be loosing money. This means that the bank makes less money, but they can offset that by offering more loans.

Investors don't want to buy single mortgage investments

Someone with $100M doesn't want to piddle around $100K at a time, so they buy groups of mortgages. The banks in turn group mortgages into categories of risk, so the investors can weigh risk vs. reward, and buy these groups of mortgages accordingly. To prevent the banks from lying, there are rating agencies that give these bundles ratings so investors can judge risk.

Banks have too many low quality loans to sell

So they start mixing the high risk loans into groups of low risk loans. The problem is they don't change the package risk rating to reflect this lower quality mix

Investors don't want to hold all this risk

So they start selling shares in their companies that trade in packages of mortgages, or start mixing these mortgages into larger investments. So people are buying shares of a black box of loans and shares containing mislabeled packages, created by a bank that is offering too many loans to people who should not have them.

Now we have a situation where 100s of billions of dollars are being traded which are tied to high risk loans.

Tree of Blame

  1. Baby Boomers getting loans they cannot afford - Not a big deal, as this happens all the time, and is absorbed by the risk calculation that banks do when offering loans
  2. Banks offering too many loans to people who cannot afford them. - This is an issue because bank deposits are backed by the FDIC. However, in the grand scheme of things, this only becomes a problem when done on a HUGE scale.
  3. Rating agencies applied great ratings to packages of mortgages that were really sub-par. - Big Deal. Huge problem. Very underhanded, and these people should be thrown in jail.
  4. Traders are selling really complicated investment structures that include these risky loans. - This isn't such a sleezy thing to do, but it needs to become illegal. The reason is that people who are buying these packages don't really have any way to understand what is actually inside them, so it's all done on trust. This concentrates the point of failure onto the rating agency who in this case lied about the quality of the packages.

Summary

If baby boomers didn't try to get loans they couldn't afford, sure, we would have avoided this mess. But the more critical problems were:

  1. The number of crap loans given by these huge banks.
  2. The lies from the rating agency.
  3. The complex derivatives that made it so no person could see the issue.

• Wall Street: Moral Hazard

  • Government: Regulation

  • Banking is a regulated industry. The safeguards and regulations that were in place were ineffective in preventing the sort of disaster regulation is meant to avoid. The regulators were far too cozy with the industry, in thrall to them and personally benefited from letting matters slide.

  • Eventually, the liabilities taken on by the largest banks became so huge that those at the top of the banks knew the government could not allow them to fail, which encouraged them to be ever more reckless.

Wall Street didn't care about or focus on the bigger picture. The people involved looked only at whether they themsleves were profiting from transactions in which they were involved. In every case you examine, it can be seen that people layed the responsibility for negative outcomes at somebody else's door. Also, during every trade from the bottom to the top, from the home buyer, all the way up to the investment banks, people were making money on the deal.

Here is a typical example illustrating the way things were going down all the way along the chain: Rating Agencies. There are a couple of big agencies, "Moody's" and "Standard & Poor". The way they make money is by taking fees for examining a stock and then assigning a rating to it, indicating how risky it is. US Government Bonds get a triple AAA rating, whereas bonds from a struggling country would receive a lower rating. It was a convenient system, a bit like Michelin stars for restaurants, and big companies were jealous of their good rating.

What went wrong? Well, you know how easier it is for a professor to give out "A" grades to everybody? If they give somebody a poor grade, there are complaints, and then everybody complains, so everybody gets an "A", and you end up with grade inflation and an "A" grade not meaning much at all. The same thing happened with stocks. A company would go to a rating agency and say, "Rate my stock", but the agency would know that if they didn't give it a high rating, then the next time, the company would just go to the other agency, and they would lose their fees. (And here is an important part, also the individual making the rating would lose their own "personal money", from not getting a commission / getting fired for losing a client.)

Soon, rating agencies were giving out high ratings for even terrible stocks. Why raise the issue with your boss? You would be rocking the boat, and losing personal money. In the end, when people started asking questions, the agencies took the position that they were not liable for providing these ratings, they were not guaranteeing them in any way. They were, they said, just offering their opinions. It was up to the market to decide whether to accept their opinions, caveat emptor, "buyer beware".

Before everything fell apart, people in the industry were becoming aware that all could not be right with things, in this case, the veracity of the ratings. It was in nobody's self interest to do anything about that issue, though. If it were considered at all, it was seen as somebody else's problem, or just the way things were or an aberration that would self-correct, or, more often than not, something which could be exploited for financial gain.

What is strangest yet, is that those banks which caused to problems before, the "too big to fail" banks, are now even larger than they were before the crisis. Also, the opportunity to regulate more strictly or break up the big banks altogether has been lost. They are still too influential, resist being cut down to size and lobby against it. I think that a similar banking crisis is likely to happen again. If that does occur, I hope that the government goes to congress again to raise the billions it needs (trillions!) and then lets the banks fail. They should use the money to provide liquidity to new banks that arise in their place in a hopefully more regulated market.

A readable account explaining the banking crisis, "The Big Short" has been made into a film. There are now some good documentaries on the topic, too.
